title: Stable Deep Reinforcement Learning via Isotropic Gaussian Representations
claim: Without structure, tracking error can grow and shrink non-monotonically; with isotropic structure it always shrinks, giving stable convergence.
layout: 2 side-by-side 2-D vector sketches, orange titles, red curve through arrow tips
description: Two side-by-side 2-D coordinate-axis sketches with orange titles. The left title reads 'Γ-dot could be positive or negative' and the right reads 'Γ-dot is always negative'. In each panel, blue arrows labeled e1 to e4 fan out from the origin. A red curve passes through the arrow tips. In the left panel the arrows point in irregular directions and have very different lengths, and the red curve wanders with kinks and reversals. The arrows are drawn as two groups, one on each side of the vertical axis. In the right panel the arrows are arranged in a smooth, symmetric fan and the red curve forms a clean, nested, butterfly-like shape that narrows toward the origin. The eye goes first to the orange titles, then to the contrast between the tangled left curve and the smooth right curve.
caption: Illustration of two tracking regimes. Left: the norm of the tracking error exhibits non-monotonic behavior and fails to converge, indicating unstable tracking. Right: the tracking error decreases monotonically and converges to zero, corresponding to stable tracking dynamics.
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning systems often suffer from unstable training dynamics due to non-stationarity, where learning objectives and data distributions evolve over time. We show that under non-stationary targets, isotropic Gaussian embeddings are provably advantageous. In particular, they induce stable tracking of time-varying targets for linear readouts, achieve maximal entropy under a fixed variance budget, and encourage a balanced use of all representational dimensions--all of which enable agents to be more adaptive and stable. Building on this insight, we propose the use of Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization for shaping representations toward an isotropic Gaussian distribution during training. We demonstrate empirically, over a variety of domains, that this simple and computationally inexpensive method improves performance under non-stationarity while reducing representation collapse, neuron dormancy, and training instability.
